questions.q: Besides the model's own weights, what else must fit in GPU memory at the same time during training?
options: Gradients, optimizer state, and activations — all held in VRAM alongside the weights
Nothing else; only the trained weights need to be on the GPU during training
Only the training dataset's raw text files
The GPU driver source code
questions.explain: Training requires weights, gradients (one value per parameter), optimizer state (e.g. Adam's momentum and variance), and activations from the forward pass to all reside in VRAM simultaneously.

questions.q: Why is 'CUDA out of memory' described as the most common training failure, rather than the job simply running too slowly?
options: Because GPU clock speed degrades over time and eventually halts training

Because the combined working set — weights, gradients, optimizer state, and activations — frequently exceeds the VRAM physically installed on the card, which stops the job outright rather than just slowing it down
Because Python raises this error whenever a script has a syntax error
Because cloud providers intentionally throttle memory to force customers onto larger instances
questions.explain: Unlike a slow job that still finishes, running out of VRAM capacity stops training entirely — which is why memory, not raw compute speed, is the more common practical constraint.

questions.q: In the worked example, why can fine-tuning a 7B-parameter model need 80-100+ GB of VRAM when the FP16 weights alone are only about 14 GB?
options: Because FP16 training always doubles the stated model size for no specific reason
Because the GPU reserves half its memory for the operating system
Because gradients (~14 GB) and Adam's FP32 optimizer state (~56 GB, from momentum and variance per parameter) stack on top of the weights, plus additional activation memory
Because the dataset itself must be fully loaded into VRAM
questions.explain: Gradients roughly match the weights in size, and Adam's optimizer state (kept in FP32 for stability) is often the single largest consumer — together with activations, this is why the real memory footprint is far larger than the weights alone.

questions.q: What is gradient checkpointing used for?
options: Saving model weights to disk at regular intervals for backup purposes
Checking that gradients sum to zero before an optimizer step
Compressing gradients for faster network transfer between GPUs
Recomputing activations during the backward pass instead of storing all of them during the forward pass, trading extra compute time for reduced memory usage
questions.explain: Gradient checkpointing discards most activations after the forward pass and recomputes them as needed during backprop, directly reducing the memory pressure that causes out-of-memory failures.

questions.q: What is the difference between GPU memory capacity and GPU memory bandwidth?
options: Capacity is how much total VRAM is on the card (determining whether a workload fits at all); bandwidth is how fast data moves between that memory and the compute cores (determining whether cores sit idle waiting on data)
They are two names for the exact same specification
Capacity only matters for inference, and bandwidth only matters for training
Bandwidth refers to network bandwidth between separate GPU servers, unrelated to a single card's memory
questions.explain: Capacity (e.g. 80 GB on an A100-80GB) decides if a job's working set fits; bandwidth (e.g. ~2 TB/s via HBM2e) decides how fast that memory can feed the thousands of parallel compute cores. A job can be bound by either, and the fixes differ.
